newsitem.title: UK: Tax receipts to boost July UK public finances.
newsitem.headline: Tax receipts to boost July UK public finances.

text.p: Britain's public sector deficit is expected to shrink by just under two billion pounds ($3.2 billion) in July as revenues are buoyed by an influx of VAT payments and corporation tax receipts.

A Reuter poll of economists suggested July saw a public sector debt repayment of 1.9 billion stg as tax receipts outstripped spending. This compares with June's larger-than-expected PSBR (Public Sector Borrowing Requirement) of 4.75 billion stg.
The data are due on Monday at 0830 GMT.

"The main reason for this is the culmination of a number of due dates for tax receipts, namely value-added tax (VAT) and a large inflow of corporation tax," said Mark Wall, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
NatWest Markets' UK economist John O'Sullivan said changes in VAT payment rules mean this year would see substantial inflows of cash in the month at the beginning of each quarter.
Analysts said government spending was still under tight control and this was also acting as positive for debt repayment, but the main impact was coming from the strong revenue side.
"The spending side continues to be quite good, but basically it's a revenue story," said John O'Sullivan, UK economist at Natwest Markets.
The public finances have been boosted this year by robust high street spending which showed no signs of abating in July.
"It's a big year for consumer spending, especially on durable goods and those durable goods are subject to VAT," O'Sullivan said.
Retail sales data for July have not yet been released, but a survey from the British Retail Consortium suggested sales grew at their fastest rate for nine months in July.

July's repayment is forecast to come in roughly in line with July 1996's repayment of 1.84, but HSBC Market's economist Jonathan Loynes said last July's repayment was swollen by privatisation proceeds, which would not be repeated this year.
"Accordingly, this July's expected repayment figure would represent a significant improvement on an underlying basis," he said.

And while predicting a healthy debt repayment for July, economists said the repayment would have been even larger but for the introduction of income tax self-assessment for the self-employed. The new rules will shift some of July's usually large income tax take into August.
"It would be a bigger repayment were it not for the fact that the twice annual self-employment tax receipt income now comes in August rather than July," O'Sullivan said.
Economists said prospects were encouraging for the government hitting its 1997/98 PSBR target, which Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown put at 10.9 billion pounds in his July 2 budget.

"They're looking good for around 11 billion. I think there will be a bit of an overrun on the spending side, but we also think they'll get a little more buoyant revenue than they're going for," O'Sullivan said.
